 Hyundai Recalls Nearly 38,000 Vehicles Over Air Bag Failure Risk — Check These Models
 Daniel Webster 2026년 11월 9일 월 오후 1:14 UTC 0 Hyundai is recalling approximately 37,901 Veloster N and Kona Electric vehicles because a software defect could prevent airbags and seat belt pretensioners from activating during a crash. Jonathan Weiss/Shutterstock Quick Read 
 Hyundai is recalling 37,901 vehicles because a software defect could prevent airbags and seat belt pretensioners from activating during a crash.
 The recall affects certain 2019–2022 Hyundai Veloster N and 2019–2023 Hyundai Kona Electric vehicles.
 Hyundai dealerships will update the airbag control unit software free of charge, with owner notification letters expected beginning January 1, 2027.
 Owners can check their vehicle identification number (VIN) at NHTSA.gov/recalls or contact Hyundai at 1-855-371-9460.
 Nearly 38,000 Hyundai vehicles are being recalled over a software defect that could leave drivers and passengers without critical protection during a collision. The problem affects airbags and seat belt pretensioners, two safety systems designed to reduce the risk of serious injuries when a crash occurs.
 The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) identifies the recall as campaign number 26V728000, covering certain Hyundai Veloster N and Kona Electric vehicles manufactured across multiple model years.
 Unlike recalls involving mechanical components that wear out over time, this issue involves software within the vehicle’s airbag control unit. Hyundai has identified a free software update as the remedy, but owners should verify whether their vehicles are affected rather than assuming the problem doesn’t apply to them.
 Here’s what Hyundai drivers need to know about the recall, the potential safety consequences, and how to arrange repairs.
 Which Hyundai Vehicles Are Being Recalled?
 Hyundai Motor America is recalling approximately 37,901 vehicles across two model lines because of the potential airbag control unit malfunction. The affected models include certain 2019, 2020, 2021, and 2022 Hyundai Veloster N vehicles, along with certain 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023 Hyundai Kona Electric vehicles. According to the official NHTSA recall database , the campaign is identified as 26V728000, while Hyundai uses internal recall number 311. Not every vehicle manufactured during these model years is necessarily included, because recall eligibility depends on specific production and vehicle identification information. Owners should check their individual VIN before scheduling service rather than relying solely on the model year.

 The Software Defect Could Prevent Critical Safety Systems From Working
 The problem involves the air bag control unit, commonly called the ACU, which helps manage the deployment of occupant-restraint systems during a collision. Hyundai’s recall documentation indicates that a software error may improperly deactivate the airbag system and seat belt pretensioners. Seat belt pretensioners are designed to tighten the seat belt during certain crashes, helping restrain occupants and position them for the protective action of other safety systems. If the affected systems fail to activate when needed, drivers and passengers could face an increased risk of injury. The recall does not establish that every affected vehicle will experience a failure, but the possibility is serious enough to warrant a manufacturer safety recall.

 Hyundai Will Fix the Problem at No Cost
 The remedy identified in Hyundai’s recall announcement is an update to the airbag control unit software performed by an authorized Hyundai dealership. Owners will not be charged for the recall-related software update, regardless of whether their vehicle is still covered by its original factory warranty. Because the problem involves software, the announced remedy does not require replacing the entire air bag system or seat belt assemblies. However, owners should contact their dealership to confirm when the update will be available for their particular vehicle and how long the service appointment is expected to take. Keeping a copy of the completed repair order can also provide documentation that the safety recall was addressed.
 Don’t Wait Until January to Check Your Vehicle
 Hyundai expects to begin mailing owner notification letters on January 1, 2027, explaining the recall and the steps needed to obtain repairs. However, the affected VINs were scheduled to become searchable through NHTSA’s recall database beginning November 6, 2026, allowing owners to check their vehicles before receiving a letter. Drivers can find their 17-character VIN near the bottom of the windshield on the driver’s side, on the driver’s door-jamb label, or in their registration paperwork. Entering that number at NHTSA.gov/recalls can help identify open safety recalls associated with the vehicle. Owners can also contact Hyundai customer service at 1-855-371-9460 and reference recall number 311 to request information about their vehicle’s eligibility and repair arrangements.
 Is It Safe to Keep Driving an Affected Hyundai?
 The published recall record does not include a specific federal “Do Not Drive” instruction for vehicles covered by this campaign. However, that does not mean the software defect is insignificant, because air bags and seat belt pretensioners are important components of a vehicle’s occupant-protection system. Owners should contact Hyundai or an authorized dealership for guidance about their particular vehicle, especially if an air bag warning light is illuminated or another restraint-system problem is suspected. Drivers should not attempt to modify the air bag control unit software themselves or assume that the absence of dashboard warnings guarantees the system will function properly in a crash. Scheduling the manufacturer’s free remedy as soon as it becomes available is the most direct way to address the identified safety concern.
 A Free Recall Repair Could Prevent a Much Bigger Problem
 Vehicle recalls are not simply administrative notices, particularly when they involve equipment designed to protect occupants during serious accidents. Hyundai’s latest recall affects nearly 38,000 vehicles that may have a software problem capable of interfering with airbag and seat belt pretensioner deployment. Although the manufacturer has identified a free software update, owners must still determine whether their vehicles are included and arrange for the repair. Checking a VIN takes only a few minutes and can help identify other outstanding safety recalls that may also require attention. If you own a Hyundai Veloster N or Kona Electric from the affected model years, verifying your recall status now could help ensure critical safety equipment works as intended when it matters most.
